text: You've run init, plan, and apply. Now the question is what Terraform is actually keeping track of while it does that. This lesson covers two block types you'll write constantly — resource and data — and the state file that makes the whole workflow possible in the first place.

A resource block is an instruction: create this, and manage it from now on. azurerm_resource_group is the resource type, defined by the azurerm provider; rg is the local name you reference elsewhere as azurerm_resource_group.rg; the body sets its real properties. Once applied, Terraform considers this resource group its own — delete the block and apply again, and Terraform destroys the real thing to match. That ownership is the entire point of a resource block.

A data source looks similar but means something very different: it reads information about something that already exists, and Terraform never creates, changes, or destroys it. data.azurerm_resource_group.existing looks up a resource group some other process already created and exposes its real attributes, like location, so this configuration can reuse them. Delete that data block and reapply, and nothing happens to the real resource group — Terraform just stops reading it.

So the distinction in one line: resource means manage this, data means tell me about this. And underneath both of them sits terraform.tfstate, a JSON file Terraform writes every time you apply, recording every resource it manages and the last real-world values it knows for each one — IDs, computed attributes, dependency relationships.

You can look at state, but you should never hand-edit it. terraform state list shows every resource currently tracked, and terraform state show azurerm_resource_group.rg shows one resource's full recorded detail — those are the supported ways in.

Here's the single most important mechanical fact in Terraform: plan and apply diff your configuration against state, not directly against whatever's actually running in Azure. Most providers do refresh state from the real API during plan, which is why someone changing a resource by hand usually does get caught as drift — but the comparison that decides what to create, update, or destroy is always config versus state. Lose that file, and Terraform loses its memory of what it's managing. Next lesson: the HCL building blocks — variables, outputs, and locals — that every real configuration uses.
